@graph.name: Merge, Divert and Sorting
@graph.description: Merge and divert conveyors are the routing part of a conveyor line: a merge combines cases from several lines onto one path, a divert sends a case to another lane, sorting directs each case to its destination and a reject station removes nonconforming units. TRF Industrial Automation engineers these modules inside TRFIntraflow, always as part of a complete line.

mainEntity.name: Can Several Packaging Lines Share One Palletizer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Merge modules bring the lines onto one path, with buffers and metering that give each line its turn, so a stop on one line does not have to stop the others, and sorting helps keep SKUs from mixing on the pallet. The sharing logic is engineered together with the palletizer interface: TRFSpeed is built to consolidate the flow of several lines, and a custom palletizer covers layouts beyond the standard platforms.

mainEntity.name: Does Sorting Require a Warehouse Management System?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Sorting can run on the product data read from the case and on rules held in the conveyor PLC. Where the plant uses a warehouse management system, TRFIntraflow includes WMS and warehouse interfaces, so the routing rules can come from the plant's logistics system. That interface is defined during project engineering with the plant's IT team.

mainEntity.name: Can a Conveyor System Integrate With My Palletizer and Case Packer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Routing modules carry each case from the machine that packs it, such as TRFRapidpack, TRFOnepack or TRFDroppack, to the palletizer or position that receives it, through defined interfaces. Signals such as lane full, palletizer ready and case rejected are engineered once, in a single control concept.

mainEntity.name: Which Industries Use Merge and Divert Conveyors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Plants with several packaging lines or many SKUs use them the most, including food processing, protein processing, personal care, CPG, beverage and pet food manufacturers.

mainEntity.name: What Information Is Needed to Design a Routing System?

acceptedAnswer.text: Layout drawings, line rates, case dimensions and weights, the number of lines and destinations, the way cases are identified and the equipment the conveyors must connect to. A list of your SKUs and the routing rules you use today is often the most useful document to start with. The application review turns this into the module arrangement and the control logic.
